# Before You Try to Go Deep

If you're so flooded that you can't stay in the room and make a choice you can actually follow through on, this probably isn't the moment to dig deeper. Get some support around you first. You can come back to the inner-child conversation later.

## You Don’t Need an Inner Monologue

You don't need a running voice in your head for any of this. Some people have words going almost constantly; some barely do. Even when words don't show up by themselves, you may still be able to make a sentence in your head on purpose. That's different. And if words aren't useful at all, don't force them. When I say “voice,” “ask,” or “answer,” you can say something out loud or write it, draw it, use a picture or a song, notice the sensation or urge, or just do the caring thing. Little inner speech doesn't mean vivid imagery is supposed to appear instead. Sometimes the mind is simply quiet. That isn't proof you're resisting anything.

The order isn't fixed either. In one moment the feeling comes first; in another the words do; sometimes you can't tell. You can leave a feeling wordless and come back later when words would actually help you figure out what happened, compare explanations, or decide what to do. Thinking is not automatically avoidance, and the first nonverbal feeling isn't automatically the deepest truth because it got there first.

## Regulation May Come Before Dialogue

If your body is too charged, talking may be premature. If your solar plexus, abdomen, or somewhere else feels clenched and it's hard to relax into that heart-chakra love, try a slower, non-forced exhale or some gentle massage. I love using one foot to massage the other like a Yin/Yang symbol. Circular or spiral massage over the tense area can be nice too.

Sometimes you need more bottom-up help than that: Shaking, tapping (Emotional Freedom Technique), EMDR, Brainspotting, Somatic Experiencing, Water Therapy, Massage, Energy Healing, or another approach that works from the body upward. The roadmap below puts these in sequence because the order matters.

If imagery starts pulling you away from the room you're actually in, don't close your eyes and push farther in. Keep your eyes open and stay with the room, the time, and your body. If a session leaves you functioning worse, more compelled, or less oriented afterward, make the next one shorter and get some grounded support.

### Catch the Hook Before You Interpret It

Forget naming it for a minute. Child? Protector? Something old? You can sort that out later. Maybe your jaw tightens, your belly contracts, heat comes up, or you feel yourself pull away. By the time you notice, you may already be halfway through a text or reaching for a drink; another time you're attacking, disappearing, scrolling, explaining everything, promising something, or deciding what the whole relationship means. [Pema Chödrön](https://pemachodronfoundation.org/product/taking-the-leap-book/) uses the Tibetan word *shenpa* for that tightening and urge before the whole story has finished assembling itself.

Look around. “I'm hooked.” Unless something is actually unsafe and needs action now, give it one to three breaths before you speak or do anything. Feel what's happening in your body without asking yet what it proves. Maybe the adult job right now is warmth, protection, or direction; do one small thing from there, or just let the charge settle and get on with the day. The pause doesn't mean your story is false. Something real may be happening while old stuff is mixed into it, or you may be reading the situation wrong. You do not have to decide which while you're at maximum activation. For the next ten minutes, ask the smaller question: what keeps anybody from getting hurt, and what can wait—something you want to say or send, consume, promise, or decide?

Later you can go back and ask what actually got hit. Was there a younger state or protector in it? Is there also a real grievance now? Maybe somebody crossed a boundary, maybe old history is mixed in, maybe there is grief, repair, or care you never got. Just don't upgrade a sensation into a verdict without noticing the jump. “My stomach tightened” is one thing. “That person is evil” is another. What did they actually do? What supports that conclusion, what doesn't, and what else might explain it? If there were literal words in your head at the time, keep those as part of what happened. Words you find afterward can still help you understand it, but those are words you found afterward.

None of this is an endurance test. One breath can be enough. If turning inward starts making you less oriented, less functional, or more compelled, stop and get support from outside yourself.

### Also Look Outward

Being triggered doesn't automatically mean you're wrong about what's happening. Look at the other person too. What happens when you disagree? Can they hear you without punishing you, look at what they did, take responsibility, and make room for your side? If the hard conversations keep ending with you carrying their feelings and dropping your own position, that's information. [Lindsay Gibson's work](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VlNpgFWOLPw) on emotional immaturity is useful here: stop guessing at motives for a minute and watch what the person actually does over and over. Sometimes you've already explained enough.

Don't turn one ugly conversation into a diagnosis. People are allowed to disagree with you, take time, or have a boundary of their own. What matters more is what keeps happening. Maybe they can't respond differently, maybe they won't, maybe that day they simply couldn't; sometimes you won't know. You can still stop relying on a response they aren't giving you. If their behavior changes, change your assessment. Another promise by itself isn't that change, and you don't have to keep collecting danger before you protect yourself. Guilt doesn't settle the question either. You may really have hurt somebody and need to repair it while also giving up your own position because you need their disappointment to stop.

Before you go back into the conversation, decide what would count as enough. Mutual understanding may not be available. Getting the information across or saying no and getting out without forty minutes of defending yourself may be the whole job. You don't have to make somebody understand before you act. The Witness can keep track of what's happening inside you while the Protector watches the interaction; then the Guide isn't deciding from only one side of the picture.

### Keep the Draft. Edit the Response. Care for the Writer.

Write the response you actually want to give—or just say it in your head. Don't send it yet. Then edit it as somebody who's on your side and still wants to be fair. Keep whatever in it is actually valid: the protest, responsibility that's really yours, a request or boundary, etc. “Better” doesn't necessarily mean nicer. Maybe you send the edited version. Maybe you say less, wait, or don't respond. “I need some time. I'll give you a fuller response tomorrow” can be enough if you can really keep that promise. If protection is needed now, don't postpone it because you haven't finished the exercise.

Then go back to the first draft and pay attention to the person who wrote it. What were they feeling? What were they trying so hard to get somebody else to understand? Maybe they needed protection or reassurance, or some concrete help. That first response isn't automatically childish; it may contain the most mature protest in the room. Edit the communication without turning against its author. Sending a good message and actually caring for the one who wrote the angry version are two different jobs.

### When More Processing Becomes the Hook

You can get hooked on healing too. The wound can be real while you're checking for the hundredth time whether you've finally grieved it correctly. Deal with the safety issue or practical thing that actually needs doing. Then ask what another round of processing is doing this time. Maybe you're finally feeling something you had only been thinking about, or you see something new enough that it changes what you decide or how you respond. Fine. But if you're back at the same question because the last answer didn't feel certain enough, that's a different thing. Grief can revisit familiar ground without every return being a fresh request from the child.

If it's a checking loop, let the thought sit there without debating it or trying to make it disappear and go back to the person, activity, or life you chose. You don't have to wait until it feels completely solved. Caring for the child doesn't require calling a meeting every time the mind produces a sentence.

Before another round, name what the exercise is supposed to help and what would actually be different in your life if it were working. You can leave a session calmer and full of insight while the original problem doesn't budge. If the method keeps giving you no useful contact—or mostly leaves you monitoring yourself more while daily life gets worse—don't answer that by doing more of it. Keep the part that genuinely helps and meet the need another way. The exercises here should not become a ritual you have to complete before you're allowed to live.
